items.stem: Let X₁, X₂, …, Xₙ be a random sample from Poisson(λ), with X̄ = (1/n)ΣXᵢ and S² = (1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)². Consider the statements: A. X̄ is unbiased for λ. B. S² is unbiased for λ. C. 3/10X̄ + 7/10S² is unbiased for λ. D. X̄ + S² is unbiased for λ. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: For a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance are both λ, so E(X̄) = λ and E(S²) = λ. A linear combination uX̄ + vS² then has expectation (u + v)λ, so it is unbiased exactly when u + v = 1 (negative weights are allowed). Here C has u + v = 1 and D has u + v = 2, so the true statements are A, B, C. Trap: a sum like X̄ + S² has expectation 2λ, not λ.

items.stem: Let X₁, …, Xₙ be iid with pdf f(x | θ) = 2e^(−2(x − θ)) for x ≥ θ, and 0 otherwise. Consider: A. X̄ₙ →ᵖ θ + 1/2. B. If Y = min(X₁, …, Xₙ), then f(y) = 2n e^(−2n(y − θ)), y ≥ θ. C. V(X̄ₙ) = 1/(4n). D. X̄ₙ →ᵖ θ. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: X − θ is exponential with rate λ = 2, so E(X) = θ + 1/λ = θ + 1/2 and Var(X) = 1/λ² = 1/4. Hence X̄ₙ →ᵖ θ + 1/2 (not θ) and V(X̄ₙ) = 1/4/n. The minimum exceeds y only if every observation does: P(Y > y) = e^(−nλ(y − θ)), so Y − θ is exponential with rate nλ, E(Y) = θ + 1/(nλ), and Y →ᵖ θ. True statements: A, B, C. Trap: the sample mean estimates the mean θ + 1/λ, not the start of the support θ.

items.stem: Let X₁, X₂, …, Xₙ (n ≥ 2) be iid exponential with mean θ, and let S = ΣXᵢ. Define T = 1 if X₁ > c, and 0 otherwise (c > 0 fixed). Then E[T | S] is the UMVUE of
items.explanation: T is unbiased for its own expectation: E(T) = P(X₁ > c) = e^(−c/θ). S is a complete sufficient statistic for this family, so by Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé, E[T | S] is the unique UMVUE of e^(−c/θ). Trap: the answer is what T estimates (a probability or expectation), not the parameter itself.

items.stem: In Wald's SPRT with type I error α = 0.05 and type II error β = 0.1, sampling continues while B < λₘ < A, where λₘ is the likelihood ratio L₁/L₀. Wald's approximation for the upper boundary A is
items.explanation: Wald's approximations are A ≈ (1 − β)/α and B ≈ β/(1 − α). Here A ≈ (1 − 0.1)/0.05 = 18 and B ≈ 0.1/(1 − 0.05) = 2/19. H₁ is accepted when the ratio first reaches A and H₀ when it falls to B. Trap: swapping α and β in the formulas gives 9.5.

items.stem: In Wald's SPRT with type I error α = 0.05 and type II error β = 0.1, sampling continues while B < λₘ < A, where λₘ is the likelihood ratio L₁/L₀. Wald's approximation for the lower boundary B is
items.explanation: Wald's approximations are A ≈ (1 − β)/α and B ≈ β/(1 − α). Here A ≈ (1 − 0.1)/0.05 = 18 and B ≈ 0.1/(1 − 0.05) = 2/19. H₁ is accepted when the ratio first reaches A and H₀ when it falls to B. Trap: swapping α and β in the formulas gives 1/18.

items.stem: Let h be an unbiased estimator of θ with E(h²) < ∞, and let T be a sufficient statistic. Consider the following statements: A. E(h | T) is unbiased for θ. B. Var{E(h | T)} ≤ Var(h). C. E(h | T) is the unique UMVUE of θ. D. E(h | T) does not depend on θ. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: A is true: E[E(h | T)] = E(h) = θ by the law of iterated expectations. B is true: Var(h) = Var{E(h | T)} + E{Var(h | T)}, and the last term is non-negative. C is false: uniqueness of the UMVUE needs T to be complete as well as sufficient, which is not given. D is true: the conditional distribution of the data given a sufficient T is free of θ, so E(h | T) is a genuine statistic. So the answer is A, B, D. Trap: Rao–Blackwell needs only sufficiency; Lehmann–Scheffé adds completeness to get uniqueness.

items.stem: Let h be an unbiased estimator of θ with E(h²) < ∞, and let T be a sufficient statistic. T is also complete. Consider the following statements: A. E(h | T) is unbiased for θ. B. Var{E(h | T)} ≤ Var(h). C. E(h | T) is the unique UMVUE of θ. D. E(h | T) does not depend on θ. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: A is true: E[E(h | T)] = E(h) = θ by the law of iterated expectations. B is true: Var(h) = Var{E(h | T)} + E{Var(h | T)}, and the last term is non-negative. C is true: with T complete and sufficient, Lehmann–Scheffé makes E(h | T) the unique UMVUE. D is true: the conditional distribution of the data given a sufficient T is free of θ, so E(h | T) is a genuine statistic. So the answer is A, B, C, D. Trap: Rao–Blackwell needs only sufficiency; Lehmann–Scheffé adds completeness to get uniqueness.

items.stem: Let h be an unbiased estimator of θ with E(h²) < ∞, and let T be a sufficient statistic. Consider the following statements: A. Var{E(h | T)} < Var(h) always. B. If h is already a function of T, then E(h | T) = h. C. Rao–Blackwellisation reduces variance only when T is complete. D. E(h | T) is unbiased for θ. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: A is false: equality holds when h is already a function of T. B is true: conditioning on T leaves any function of T unchanged. C is false: the variance reduction needs only sufficiency; completeness is needed for uniqueness. D is true: E[E(h | T)] = E(h) = θ by the law of iterated expectations. So the answer is B, D. Trap: Rao–Blackwell needs only sufficiency; Lehmann–Scheffé adds completeness to get uniqueness.

items.stem: Let h be an unbiased estimator of θ with E(h²) < ∞, and let T be a sufficient statistic. Consider the following statements: A. E(h | U) is an estimator for every statistic U. B. MSE{E(h | T)} ≤ MSE(h). C. E(h | T) has a smaller bias than h. D. Var{E(h | T)} ≤ Var(h). Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: A is false: if U is not sufficient, E(h | U) can depend on θ and then is not a statistic at all. B is true: conditioning keeps the mean and cannot increase the variance, so the mean squared error cannot rise. C is false: conditioning keeps the expectation, so the bias is unchanged (here both are unbiased). D is true: Var(h) = Var{E(h | T)} + E{Var(h | T)}, and the last term is non-negative. So the answer is B, D. Trap: Rao–Blackwell needs only sufficiency; Lehmann–Scheffé adds completeness to get uniqueness.

items.stem: Suppose we have X₁, …, Xₙ iid N(μ, σ²). The quantity (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n), where S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n − 1) can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: μ when σ² is known only
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. It has a t distribution with n − 1 df whatever μ and σ are, and it contains only μ as an unknown, so it gives intervals for μ without knowing σ. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have X₁, …, Xₙ iid N(μ, σ²). The quantity Σ(Xᵢ − μ)²/σ² can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. It is χ² with n df, free of the parameters, but computing it needs μ, so it serves for σ² only when μ is known. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have X₁, …, Xₙ iid N(μ, σ²). The quantity (n − 1)S²/σ² can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: neither μ nor σ²: it is not a pivot
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. It is χ² with n − 1 df and involves only σ² (μ is estimated by X̄ inside S²), so it gives intervals for σ² with μ unknown. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have X₁, …, Xₙ iid Uniform(0, θ). The quantity X₍ₙ₎/θ, where X₍ₙ₎ is the sample maximum can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: θ only when n is large
no parameter: its distribution depends on θ
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. P(X₍ₙ₎/θ ≤ t) = tⁿ on (0, 1) whatever θ is, so it is a pivot and can be inverted for θ. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have X₁, …, Xₙ iid with pdf λe^(−λx), x > 0. The quantity 2λΣXᵢ can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: λ only when n is large
no parameter: its distribution depends on λ
the mean only when λ is known
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. 2λΣXᵢ is χ² with 2n df for every λ, so it is an exact pivot for λ. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have X₁, …, Xₙ iid exponential with mean θ. The quantity ΣXᵢ/θ can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: θ only when n is large
no parameter: its distribution depends on θ
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. ΣXᵢ/θ has a Gamma(n, 1) distribution free of θ, so it is a pivot for θ. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have X₁, …, Xₙ iid N(μ, σ²) with σ unknown. The quantity X̄ − μ can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: no parameter: its distribution depends on the unknown σ
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. X̄ − μ ~ N(0, σ²/n), so its distribution involves the unknown σ; it is not a pivot until it is divided by S/√n. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have independent samples from N(μ₁, σ²) and N(μ₂, σ²), sizes m and n, common σ² unknown. The quantity [(X̄ − Ȳ) − (μ₁ − μ₂)]/[Sₚ√(1/m + 1/n)], with Sₚ² the pooled variance can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: no parameter: its distribution depends on σ²
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. It has a t distribution with m + n − 2 df whatever the parameters are, so it is a pivot for the difference in means. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have independent samples from N(μ₁, σ₁²) and N(μ₂, σ₂²), sizes m and n. The quantity (S₁²/σ₁²)/(S₂²/σ₂²) can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: no parameter: its distribution depends on σ₁ and σ₂
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. It has an F distribution with (m − 1, n − 1) df free of all parameters, and it involves only the ratio σ₁²/σ₂². Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.

items.stem: Suppose we have X₁, …, Xₙ iid with pdf e^(−(x − θ)), x > θ. The quantity X₍₁₎ − θ, where X₍₁₎ is the sample minimum can be used as a pivot to obtain a confidence interval for
options: θ only when n is large
no parameter: its distribution depends on θ
items.explanation: A pivot is a function of the data and the parameter whose distribution does not depend on any unknown parameter. X₍₁₎ − θ is exponential with rate n for every θ, so it is a pivot and gives exact intervals for θ. Trap: a quantity whose distribution still involves an unknown nuisance parameter is not a pivot.
